[[File:Berge's theorem.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|A [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]], denoted in blue, is shown to ''not'' be a [[maximum cardinality matching]] because of the presence of an '''augmenting path''', with endpoints at the yellow vertices.]]

{{about|the theorem in graph theory|Berge's maximum theorem|Maximum theorem}}
In [[graph theory]], '''Berge's theorem''' states that a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] ''M'' in a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] ''G'' is [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum]] (contains the largest possible number of edges) if and only if there is no '''augmenting path''' (a path that starts and ends on free (unmatched) vertices, and alternates between edges in and not in the matching) with ''M''.

It was proven by [[France|French]] mathematician [[Claude Berge]] in 1957 (though already observed by [[Julius Petersen|Petersen]] in 1891 and [[Dénes Kőnig|Kőnig]] in 1931).

== Proof ==
To prove Berge's theorem, we first need a [[Lemma (mathematics)|lemma]].  Take a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] ''G'' and let ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'' be two [[Matching (graph theory)|matchings]] in ''G''.  Let ''{{prime|G}}'' be the resultant [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] from taking the [[symmetric difference]] of ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}''; i.e. (''M'' - ''{{prime|M}}'') ∪ (''{{prime|M}}'' - ''M'').  ''{{prime|G}}'' will consist of connected components that are one of the following:
# An isolated [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertex]].
# An even [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycle]] whose edges alternate between ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}''.
# A [[Path (graph theory)|path]] whose edges alternate between ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'', with distinct endpoints.

The lemma can be proven by observing that each [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertex]] in ''{{prime|G}}'' can be incident to at most 2 edges: one from ''M'' and one from ''{{prime|M}}''.  Graphs where every vertex has degree less than or equal to 2 must consist of either isolated [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]], [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]], and [[Path (graph theory)|paths]].  Furthermore, each path and cycle in ''{{prime|G}}'' must alternate between ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}''.  In order for a [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycle]] to do this, it must have an equal number of edges from ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'', and therefore be of even length.

Let us now prove the [[contrapositive]] of Berge's theorem: ''G'' has a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] larger than ''M'' if and only if ''G'' has an augmenting path. Clearly, an augmenting path ''P'' of ''G'' can be used to produce a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] ''{{prime|M}}'' that is larger than ''M'' — just take ''{{prime|M}}'' to be the [[symmetric difference]] of ''P'' and ''M'' (''{{prime|M}}'' contains exactly those edges of ''G'' that appear in exactly one of ''P'' and ''M''). Hence, the reverse direction follows.

For the forward direction, let ''{{prime|M}}'' be a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] in ''G'' larger than ''M''. Consider ''D'', the symmetric difference of ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}''. Observe that ''D'' consists of paths and even [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]] (as observed by the earlier lemma). Since ''{{prime|M}}'' is larger than ''M'', ''D'' contains a component that has more edges from ''{{prime|M}}'' than ''M''. Such a component is a path in ''G'' that starts and ends with an edge from ''{{prime|M}}'', so it is an augmenting path.

== Corollaries ==
=== Corollary 1 ===
Let ''M'' be a maximum matching and consider an alternating chain such that the edges in the path alternates between being and not being in ''M''.  If the alternating chain is a [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycle]] or a [[Path (graph theory)|path]] of even length starting on an unmatched vertex, then a new maximum matching ''{{prime|M}}'' can be found by interchanging the edges found in ''M'' and not in ''M''.  For example, if the alternating chain is (''m''<sub>1</sub>, ''n''<sub>1</sub>, ''m''<sub>2</sub>, ''n''<sub>2</sub>, ...), where ''m''<sub>i</sub> ∈ ''M'' and ''n''<sub>i</sub> ∉ ''M'', interchanging them would make all ''n''<sub>i</sub> part of the new matching and make all ''m''<sub>i</sub> not part of the matching.

=== Corollary 2 ===
An edge is considered "free" if it belongs to a maximum matching  but does not belong to all maximum matchings.  An edge ''e'' is free if and only if, in an arbitrary maximum matching ''M'', edge ''e'' belongs to an even alternating path starting at an unmatched vertex or to an alternating [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycle]].  By the first corollary, if edge ''e'' is part of such an alternating chain, then a new maximum matching, ''{{prime|M}}'', must exist and ''e'' would exist either in ''M'' or ''{{prime|M}}'', and therefore be free.  Conversely, if edge ''e'' is free, then ''e'' is in some maximum matching ''M'' but not in ''{{prime|M}}''.  Since ''e'' is not part of both ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'', it must still exist after taking the [[symmetric difference]] of ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}''.  The [[symmetric difference]] of ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'' results in a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] consisting of isolated vertices, even alternating cycles, and alternating paths.  Suppose to the contrary that ''e'' belongs to some odd-length path component.  But then one of ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'' must have one fewer edge than the other in this component, meaning that the component as a whole is an augmenting path with respect to that matching.  By the original lemma, then, that matching (whether ''M'' or ''{{prime|M}}'') cannot be a maximum matching, which contradicts the assumption that both ''M'' and ''{{prime|M}}'' are maximum.  So, since ''e'' cannot belong to any odd-length path component, it must either be in an alternating cycle or an even-length alternating path.
